title: Mechanistic Interpretability of EEG Foundation Models via Sparse Autoencoders
claim: A four-stage modular procedure turns opaque model embeddings into interpretable, steerable, concept-grounded explanations.
layout: 4 columns, left-to-right, color-coded stage headers with text above diagrams
description: A wide figure split into four equal rounded columns, each with a colored header: blue Stage I (Spectral Decoder), green Stage II (Layer-wise SAE Training), orange Stage III (Concept Attribution), red Stage IV (Concept Steering). Each column opens with a short paragraph, then a vertical diagram. Stage I shows a Tokenizer, Transformer and Classifier strip feeding a funnel-shaped Spectral Decoder, which outputs amplitude bars and a phase dial, with a blue note box below. Stage II shows a TopK SAE with encoder and decoder trapezoids, a sparse latent bar and reconstruction vectors. Stage III shows sparse feature bars, concept icons (abnormality, age, sex, medication), a logistic regression scatter with a CAV direction, and enriched features. Stage IV is a numbered list of steps with red-highlighted feature bars and a spectral output. Color separates the stages, and the eye goes first to the headers.
caption: Pipeline overview. Starting from a frozen EEG foundation model: (Stage I) A shallow MLP spectral decoder translates token embeddings back into a human interpretable space. (Stage II) For each transformer layer, a TopK SAE recovers a sparse, over-complete feature dictionary from normalized encoder activations. (Stage III) SAE features are mapped to known clinical concepts using TCAV. (Stage IV) Concept steering substitutes the top-$n$ concept-enriched feature activations with the target-group centroid, decoding the intervention through the SAE and spectral decoder to produce a mechanistically grounded, spectrum-level explanation.
abstract: EEG foundation models achieve state-of-the-art clinical performance, yet the internal computations driving their predictions remain opaque: a barrier to clinical trust. We apply TopK Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) across three architecturally distinct EEG transformers: SleepFM, REVE, and LaBraM to extract sparse feature dictionaries from their embeddings. By grounding these features in a clinical taxonomy (abnormality, age, sex, and medication), we benchmark monosemanticity and entanglement across architectures. A single hyperparameter procedure, driven by an intrinsic dictionary health audit, transfers robustly across all three architectures. Via concept steering, we introduce a "target vs. off-target" probe area metric to quantify steering selectivity and reveal three operational regimes: selectively steerable, encoded but entangled, and non-encoded. This framework exposes critical representational failures: "wrecking-ball" interventions that collapse global model performance, and clinical entanglements, such as age-pathology confounding, where it is impossible to suppress one concept without corrupting the other. Finally, a spectral decoder maps these interventions back to the amplitude spectrum, translating latent manipulations into physiologically interpretable frequency signatures, such as pathological slow-wave suppression and $Î±$-band restoration.
